t: How To Have The Best Behaved Class In Your School
q: But with over 500 articles, five books, and three e-guides to date, it can be hard for SCM readers to determine what they are and how they work together.
The book consists of 18 short, simple lessons that anyone can learn and put into practice immediately, regardless of experience, grade level, or where you happen to teach.
It includes only what you need to know. In other words, you won’t find lengthy descriptions or any unnecessary fluff.
What you will find is the exact approach I use to turn large, challenging, and sometimes disrespectful groups of students into the polite and happy classes that I love teaching.
My promise to you is that if you earnestly follow the simple dos and don’ts presented in the book, within four weeks (or less) you’ll have the best behaved class in your school.

t: How To Stop Your Class From Calling Out
q: Before you know it, so many students are calling out without raising their hand that it becomes impossible to enforce.
Instead of lecturing or blaming your students for the disruptions, take responsibility yourself. Let them know that you haven’t done a good job protecting their right to learn.
Although it may seem silly or unnecessary, show your students exactly what raising their hand and waiting patiently to be called on looks like. It’s best to sit at a student’s desk.
Chances are, at least for a day or so, you’ll be tested. When it happens, and your students start calling out one after the other, stop everything. Just stand and wait. Take a long pause.
Another powerful strategy to break the habit of calling out is to never call on a student the moment their hand goes up. Pause first, disrupt the ‘teacher-looks-I-answer’ rhythm, then call on them.
Following the nine steps above, and being clear about when the rule isn’t in play, will remove calling out from your classroom.

t: The Difference Between False And Worthy Praise
q: False praise is praise given in order to appease, flatter, or manipulate students into doing what the teacher wants. In other words, it isn’t based on genuine accomplishment.
The beneficiary of false praise is the teacher, not the students.
So what should you say after your students complete an expectation as taught? “Thank you” will do.

Worthy praise is praise based on true accomplishment, which can be defined as new learning or effort or performance beyond what is commonly expected or what an individual student or group has done before.
The actual moment of praise may be subtle. It may be a nod from across the room or a silent fist bump. But its power to motivate and inspire students to seek taller mountains to climb has no bounds.
My firm stance on praise isn’t for the purpose of clickbait. I’m not trying to be controversial.
x: False praise, he argues, is given to manipulate students through public compliments for merely expected behavior, and it benefits the teacher rather than the student.
Argues false praise lowers the bar for what counts as excellent and can inflate students' sense of their own abilities.

Worthy praise, by contrast, is honest feedback grounded in genuine accomplishment beyond what a student has previously done, delivered quietly and only after work is complete.
Worthy praise should arrive only after work is completed and can be as subtle as a nod or fist bump.

t: Why Narration Is A Bad Classroom Management Strategy ment-strategy/
q: Even though you’re merely expressing what you see, without judgement, make no mistake: Narration is a form of false praise .
If your students know you’re going to remind them of what they need to do through narration, then there is no reason to listen closely to your initial directions.

Narration effectively teaches students that they need you to talk them through even the simplest tasks. Thus, they struggle when asked to do anything on their own, especially more complex academic work.
Because narration inhibits the development of maturity and independence and creates a weak-minded, needy class. It creates learned helplessness and a fear of failure.

Viewed from a student’s perspective, the only reason their teacher would narrate them through a simple direction is if the teacher believes they can’t do it on their own—which is the main message they receive.
x: Narration is defined as describing students' positive behavior aloud while they are performing it, and Linsin argues it is really a form of false praise.
Narration is said to weaken listening skills because students learn directions will be repeated for them via narration.
